title: A Dose of Dickens for Christian Education
author: John Mark Reynolds
summary: Classical-education writer and college founder John Mark Reynolds turns to Charles Dickens as a counter-model for Christian education, arguing that Dickens's imaginative critiques of Victorian schooling — Dotheboys Hall's brutality in Nicholas Nickleby, the street-crime consequences of educational neglect in Oliver Twist — helped England avoid the revolutionary upheaval that consumed France and Russia by making moral change possible "without turning change into the gospel." His real target is contemporary: Christian schools and colleges that reduce education to facts, definitions, and Scantron-testable content while treating discipleship, art, and wonder as optional extras. He draws a sharp line between what can be measured ("You can put facts in an online test") and what actually forms a person ("You cannot put discipleship"), arguing that any school whose decisions are driven by what software can grade or what turns a profit is "soul crushing." He closes by invoking two of Dickens's own images — the emotionally starved girl in Hard Times and the allegorical children Ignorance and Want from A Christmas Carol — as warnings about what a fact-based, credential-chasing education actually produces.
points: Reynolds credits Dickens's imaginative critiques of Victorian education and poverty (Nicholas Nickleby, Oliver Twist) with helping England avoid the revolutionary violence that consumed France and Russia, by making reform possible without messianic upheaval.

His central distinction is between what can be tested and what actually forms a person: "You can put facts in an online test. You cannot put discipleship. You can put definitions on a Scantron, but not a discussion of the text."

He warns that any school whose decisions are driven by what software can grade or what is profitable is "soul crushing," drawing an explicit parallel between being "pastored by a televangelist" and being educated by a purely content-controlled system.

He uses Dickens's own image of a girl with "a starved imagination keeping life in itself somehow" to describe the emotional cost of fact-based, content-controlled schooling that strips out joy in favor of marching through a syllabus.

He closes on Dickens's allegorical children Ignorance and Want from A Christmas Carol, arguing that "Doom is the result of education based on facts and credentials" — a direct warning aimed at Christian institutions tempted toward purely credentialist models.
quotes: He was one of the great educators of the Victorian age taking the English imagination and making change possible without turning change into the gospel.

You can put facts in an online test. You cannot put discipleship. You can put definitions on a Scantron, but not a discussion of the text. When I prepare a lecture on Dickens, I know what I know, but not what the students will ask.
Education that ever makes a decision based on what the software can do or is for profit is soul crushing. You cannot be pastored by a televangelist, and you should not be educated by one.

There was an air of jaded sullenness in them both, and particularly in the girl: yet, struggling through the dissatisfaction of her face, there was a light with nothing to rest upon, a fire with nothing to burn, a starved imagination keeping life in itself somehow, which brightened its expression.
This boy is Ignorance. This girl is Want. Beware them both, and all of their degree, but most of all beware this boy, for on his brow I see that written which is Doom, unless the writing be erased.
The fact based, content-controlled school or college strips the joy out of education for a march through the "content." This is the school that stresses the syllabus over the class experience!
